description: Solo participant at NASA Space Apps Kuala Lumpur 2026. I'm an international student in Malaysia with experience in AI/ML and data hackathons (IBM Datathon, Open Agent AI Hackathon). I'm using machine learning to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspot records into one consistent history, to better understand the fires behind Southeast Asia's yearly haze. Focus: ML, data analysis, Earth observation and clear visualization.
summary:
HazeTrace turns NASA's two fire-detecting satellite sensors into one consistent record. MODIS has counted active fires since 2000 but is ending; VIIRS, since 2012, sees smaller fires and counts several times more hotspots. Joined naively, the record shows a fake jump in 2012, so no one can tell whether a haze season is truly unusual.

I paired MODIS and VIIRS counts on a 0.25° grid for Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sarawak (2012 to 2025) and trained a LightGBM model that learns how the MODIS/VIIRS ratio changes with fire intensity, season and region. Tested on years it never saw, it has 17% lower error than a fixed conversion ratio and wins 9 of 13 years, including the 2015 record fire year. It also transfers to NOAA-20, the satellite that continues after S-NPP stopped in November 2026.

The result is a live web app (hazetrace.streamlit.app) with a satellite map, time-lapse, fire calendar and CSV downloads. It shows that 2026 had the 3rd most fire hotspots of any August to October season since 2003. It describes fire activity, not air quality.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

HazeTrace builds one comparable monthly fire-hotspot record from January 2003 to November 2026 for the haze region of Southeast Asia: Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, West and Central Kalimantan (Indonesia) and Sarawak (Malaysia). Before 2012 it uses NASA MODIS directly. From 2012 it converts VIIRS counts to what MODIS would have counted, so every year sits on the same scale and a season can be compared fairly with every season since 2003.

HOW IT WORKS

1. NASA FIRMS active-fire detections (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20) are filtered to vegetation fires and counted per 0.25° grid cell (about 28 km) and month. Near-real-time 2026 data have no fire-type flag, so persistent static sources such as gas flares are removed with a tested mask (about 2% of real fires lost, net change about 0.2%).

2. A LightGBM Poisson model, with the VIIRS count as an offset, learns the MODIS/VIIRS ratio from fire intensity (FRP), confidence, share of night detections, season, region and regional fire activity. Predicting a ratio instead of a count lets it handle record years such as 2015.

3. Validation: each year from 2013 to 2025 is hidden in turn and predicted from VIIRS alone, using the same rules as the dashboard. The model has 17% lower error than a fixed regional ratio (61 vs 73 hotspots per region-month), R² 0.97, and wins 9 of 13 years, including the 2015 record year. Applied to NOAA-20 without retraining, its error is 35 vs 43 for a fixed ratio. An independent 2026 check in Malaysia, with MODIS data never used in training, is within 22%.

THE APP

A live web dashboard (https://hazetrace.streamlit.app, code at https://github.com/maksudaakhtertumpa/hazetrace) with: a satellite map on NASA Blue Marble imagery that switches between raw VIIRS, raw MODIS and HazeTrace on one colour scale; a side-by-side view; a time-lapse of every haze season from 2003 to 2026; a fire calendar; regional rankings; real province boundaries or a custom lat/lon box; a "How good is it?" page with all validation results; and CSV downloads with a data dictionary.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Every year from August to October, smoke from these fires reaches Kuala Lumpur and Singapore. I live on the 31st floor in Kuala Lumpur and cannot open my window in haze season. Air-quality analysts, disaster officers, researchers, ESG and no-burning analysts, students and journalists need to know whether a season is truly unusual, and with MODIS ending, the long record has to continue on VIIRS. HazeTrace shows, for example, that 2026 had the 3rd most fire hotspots of any August to October season since 2003, mostly in Central Kalimantan. It supports SDG 13.1 and 13.3 (climate resilience and awareness), 15.1 and 15.3 (forests and land degradation) and 17.18 (reliable open data).

CREATIVITY

Instead of one fixed conversion factor, HazeTrace shows that the MODIS/VIIRS ratio itself changes with burning conditions (in Riau about 0.20 in 2014 to 2015 and 0.4 to 0.5 in quiet years) and learns that change. It also shows that the conversion works on a satellite it was never trained on, which keeps the record going after MODIS ends.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Honesty about limits: the app and README show where the model is weaker. A fixed ratio is about as good in Jambi, West Kalimantan and Sarawak, and in quiet years HazeTrace can fall below raw MODIS. The app warns when this happens in the selected area.

- Scope: HazeTrace describes fire activity only. It is not an air-quality reading, forecast, official alert or health advice, and it points to Malaysia DOE (APIMS), BMKG and ASMC for haze information.

- Data quality: August to November 2026 is preliminary near-real-time data and November 2026 is partial, so both are labelled and never ranked.

- Usability: tested with four student personas (geography, environmental science, remote sensing, mobile user). The fixes included a glossary, clearer labels and maps that zoom to the chosen area.

- Reproducibility: open code (MIT licence), saved results, and every number can be regenerated from NASA data.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, NumPy, LightGBM, SHAP, Shapely, Plotly, Streamlit (deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud), Git and GitHub. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery, Natural Earth boundaries. AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with code and text; all results come from running the code on NASA data.
